summary: Every California single-family home that is sold must have a working smoke alarm approved by the State Fire Marshal, and the seller has to hand the buyer a written statement saying the home complies.
alarmType: An operable smoke alarm that was approved and listed by the California State Fire Marshal and installed per his regulations at the time it was installed. A battery-operated alarm meeting the State Fire Marshal standards in force when installed counts, unless a local rule bans it. Separately, since January 1, 2014 a smoke alarm must meet State Fire Marshal listing requirements to be sold in California: it must show its date of manufacture, have a place to write the installation date, have a hush button and an end-of-life warning, and if battery-powered must contain a non-replaceable, non-removable battery good for at least 10 years. A fire alarm system with smoke detectors installed to State Fire Marshal regulations can be used instead.
coAlarms: Separate requirement, not tied to sale. The owner of any dwelling unit with a fossil-fuel-burning heater or appliance, a fireplace, or an attached garage had to install a State Fire Marshal approved CO device: by July 1, 2011 for existing single-family homes, by January 1, 2013 for other existing dwellings, and by January 1, 2016 for hotel and motel units. Number and placement must follow the new-construction building standards for that occupancy or the manufacturer's instructions. The statutory transfer disclosure form does not include a CO certification line, and failure to comply does not invalidate a transfer of title.
certification: No inspection or fire-department sign-off. The seller self-certifies: the transferor must deliver a written compliance statement to the buyer, either in the deposit receipt, an addendum, or a separate document, as soon as practicable before title transfers. The statutory Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement in Civil Code 1102.6 carries this as a seller certification that the property will have operable, approved, properly installed smoke detectors as of close of escrow. Agents and escrow are not required to monitor compliance. A failed disclosure does not void the sale; the only remedy is actual damages capped at $100 plus costs and fees.
citation: Cal. Health & Safety Code 13113.8 (smoke alarm required on sale of a single-family dwelling); HSC 13113.7 (general requirement in all dwellings); HSC 13114 (State Fire Marshal device standards, 10-year sealed battery); HSC 17926 (CO devices); Cal. Civil Code 1102.6 (transfer disclosure statement form)
lastAmended: 2012 (SB 1394, Stats. 2012, Ch. 420, chaptered September 21, 2012, amended HSC 13113.7, 13113.8, 13114 and 17926)
notVerified: Whether HSC 13113.8, 13113.7, 13114 or 17926 have been amended after 2012. The current codified text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read: plain curl returned HTTP 403 and WebFetch failed at the site, for both the section view (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=13113.8.) and the article view. The text used here is the official chaptered text of SB 1394 (2012) from leginfo.ca.gov. A later-2014 code-maintenance bill (SB 1304, Stats. 2014, Ch. 71) was checked and does not amend 13113.8, but years after 2014 were not searched exhaustively.
The State Fire Marshal's own regulations on approved alarm types and installation, and any exceptions he created to the 10-year sealed battery rule under HSC 13114(b)(2)(B), were not read.

Exemptions: HSC 13113.8(d) exempts many transfers from the written-statement duty, including court-ordered transfers, foreclosure and deed-in-lieu transfers, fiduciary transfers in estates, guardianships, conservatorships and trusts, co-owner-to-co-owner transfers, transfers to a spouse or lineal relative, divorce-related transfers, and certain tax and unclaimed-property transfers. Whether the underlying duty in subdivision (a) to have an operable alarm also falls away in those transfers was not resolved from the text.
The current wording of the Civil Code 1102.6 form was read from the 2014 chaptered version of SB 1304, not from the current code.
